code: ss_buc_independent_t(t_observed = 3, n = 20, assurance = .95) #> Error: #> ! Sample size planning is not possible with these settings. After correcting the prior study's effect for publication bias and uncertainty at the requested level of assurance, the corrected noncentrality parameter is zero, which means there is not enough information in the prior result to plan the sample size as desired. With this prior result and 'alpha_prior', the largest 'assurance' that still yields a usable plan is about .90; re-run with 'assurance' at or below that value, or raise 'alpha_prior' to lift the ceiling. Re-running at a lower 'assurance' is not free: the plan it returns carries that lower assurance, not the one you first asked for, so the long run proportion of replications reaching your target power falls accordingly. 'alpha_prior' does not change the prior study, which is what it is; it is your assumption about the publication threshold the study's literature faced, so raising it toward 1 assumes less publication bias to undo (for example, 'alpha_prior = .10' assumes the literature's journals would have published a result significant at the .10 level, a more lenient policy than .05, and 'alpha_prior = 1' assumes no publication bias at all). See Anderson, Kelley, and Maxwell (2017) and Anderson and Kelley (2024).

code: set.seed(2017)  true_d <- 0.2     # the true (small) population effect n      <- 30      # participants per group in each study G      <- 1000    # number of studies the field runs  studies <- replicate(G, {   control   <- rnorm(n, mean = 0,      sd = 1)   treatment <- rnorm(n, mean = true_d, sd = 1)   tt <- t.test(treatment, control, var.equal = TRUE)   # For equal n per group, Cohen's d = t * sqrt(2 / n).   c(t = unname(tt$statistic), p = tt$p.value,     d = unname(tt$statistic) * sqrt(2 / n)) }) studies <- as.data.frame(t(studies)) studies$published <- studies$p < .05 power.t.test(delta = true_d, n = n, sig.level = .05)$power #> [1] 0.1154342 p_published <- mean(studies$published) c(proportion = p_published,   mcse       = sqrt(p_published * (1 - p_published) / G)) #> proportion       mcse  #>   0.126000   0.010494 d_published <- studies$d[studies$published] rbind(all       = c(mean = mean(studies$d),                     mcse = sd(studies$d) / sqrt(G)),       published = c(mean = mean(d_published),                     mcse = sd(d_published) / sqrt(length(d_published)))) #>                mean        mcse #> all       0.1904788 0.008310797 #> published 0.6166919 0.013018500

1, ncp = ncp) - (1 + C) / 2,           c(0, 10), tol = 1e-10)$root } # Ordinary power of a paired t test with n pairs, at a noncentrality # parameter stated for the prior study's N pairs. power_at <- function(n, ncp) {   crit <- qt(.975, df = n - 1)   delta <- ncp * sqrt(n / N)   (1 - pt(crit, df = n - 1, ncp = delta)) + pt(-crit, df = n - 1, ncp = delta) } safeguard_n <- function(ncp) {   n <- 2   while (power_at(n, ncp) < .80) n <- n + 1   n } limit_60 <- lower_limit(.60) plan_sg <- ss_buc_paired_t(t_observed = t_obs, N = N, alpha_prior = 1,                            assurance = .80) data.frame(method = c("safeguard power", "BUCSS, alpha_prior = 1"),            ncp = c(limit_60, row_value(plan_sg, "ncp_adjusted")),            necessary_N = c(safeguard_n(limit_60),                            row_value(plan_sg, "necessary_N"))) #>                   method      ncp necessary_N #> 1        safeguard power 2.069878          57 #> 2 BUCSS, alpha_prior = 1 2.069874          57 levels_C <- c(.60, .80, .90) data.frame(   confidence_level = levels_C,   assurance = (1 + levels_C) / 2,   interval_lower_limit = sapply(levels_C, lower_limit),   ncp_adjusted = sapply(levels_C, function(C) {     plan <- ss_buc_paired_t(t_observed = t_obs, N = N, alpha_prior = 1,                             assurance = (1 + C) / 2)     row_value(plan, "ncp_adjusted")   })) #>   confidence_level assurance interval_lower_limit ncp_adjusted #> 1              0.6      0.80             2.069878     2.069874 #> 2              0.8      0.90             1.598418     1.598360 #> 3              0.9      0.95             1.209421     1.208942 p_prior <- c(.01, .05, .10, .15) t_prior <- qt(1 - 2)   delta <- d * sqrt(n / 2)   (1 - pt(crit, df = 2 * n - 2, ncp = delta)) +     pt(-crit, df = 2 * n - 2, ncp = delta) } # Safeguard power with the 60% limit read on 'df' and restated as a # standardized mean difference by the factor 'to_d'. safeguard_ind <- function(df, to_d) {   limit <- uniroot(function(ncp) pt(3, df = df, ncp = ncp) - .80, c(0, 10),                    tol = 1e-10)$root   n <- 2   while (power_ind(n, limit * to_d) < .80) n <- n + 1   n } harmonic <- 2 * prod(n_prior) / sum(n_prior) plan_unequal <- ss_buc_independent_t(t_observed = 3, n = n_prior,                                      alpha_prior = 1, assurance = .80) data.frame(   prior_read_as = c("groups of 4 and 100, df 102", "7 per group, df 12",                     "8 per group, df 14", "BUCSS, alpha_prior = 1"),   necessary_n_per_group = c(     safeguard_ind(sum(n_prior) - code: ss_buc_chisq_diff(chisq_observed = 9.5, N = 250, df_full = 42, df_restricted = 43,                   alpha_prior = .05, alpha_planned = .05, assurance = .80,                   desired_power = .80) ss_buc_chisq_diff(chisq_observed = 9.5, N = 250, df_full = 0, df_restricted = 43) #> Error: #> ! 'df_full' is 0, so the full model is saturated and this comparison is the restricted model's omnibus test of model fit, not a difference test between two substantive models. This function does not apply to an omnibus fit chi square: the correction assumes a literature publishes significant results, whereas a publishable fit chi square is a small (nonsignificant) one, which inverts the selection region the method is built on. A just-identified full model also has 0 degrees of freedom; if that is your case and the comparison is a genuine difference test, the plan depends only on the number of constraints, so call with 'df_full = 1' and 'df_restricted' equal to 1 plus the number of constraints.

code: result <- ss_buc_R2(F_observed = 5, N = 150, p = 4, alpha_prior = .05,   alpha_planned = .05, assurance = .80, desired_power = .80) result #>  term              value  #>  necessary_N       234    #>  actual_power      0.8    #>  ncp_adjusted      7.82   #>  R2_planning       0.0495 #>  F_observed        5      #>  N                 150    #>  p                 4      #>  random_predictors 0      #>  alpha_prior       0.05   #>  alpha_planned     0.05   #>  assurance         0.8    #>  desired_power     0.8    #>  #> Design: Multiple regression: omnibus test of model R2 #> Predictors: fixed by design #> Sample size unit: total #> Largest supportable assurance: .98  # Predictors sampled along with the outcome, as in most observational # research: ss_buc_R2(F_observed = 5, N = 150, p = 4, random_predictors = TRUE) #>  term              value  #>  necessary_N       239    #>  actual_power      0.801  #>  ncp_adjusted      7.76   #>  R2_planning       0.0492 #>  F_observed        5      #>  N                 150    #>  p                 4      #>  random_predictors 1      #>  alpha_prior       0.05   #>  alpha_planned     0.05   #>  assurance         0.8    #>  desired_power     0.8    #>  #> Design: Multiple regression: omnibus test of model R2 #> Predictors: random (sampled along with the outcome) #> Sample size unit: total #> Largest supportable assurance: .98  # Requesting more assurance than the prior result can support stops with an # informative error naming the largest workable assurance (here near .98): try(ss_buc_R2(F_observed = 5, N = 150, p = 4, assurance = .99)) #> Error : Sample size planning is not possible with these settings. After correcting the prior study's effect for publication bias and uncertainty at the requested level of assurance, the corrected noncentrality parameter is zero, which means there is not enough information in the prior result to plan the sample size as desired. With this prior result and 'alpha_prior', the largest 'assurance' that still yields a usable plan is about .98; re-run with 'assurance' at or below that value, or raise 'alpha_prior' to lift the ceiling. Re-running at a lower 'assurance' is not free: the plan it returns carries that lower assurance, not the one you first asked for, so the long run proportion of replications reaching your target power falls accordingly. 'alpha_prior' does not change the prior study, which is what it is; it is your assumption about the publication threshold the study's literature faced, so raising it toward 1 assumes less publication bias to undo (for example, 'alpha_prior = .10' assumes the literature's journals would have published a result significant at the .10 level, a more lenient policy than .05, and 'alpha_prior = 1' assumes no publication bias at all). See Anderson, Kelley, and Maxwell (2017) and Anderson and Kelley (2024).

After correcting the prior study's effect for publication bias and uncertainty at the requested level of assurance, the corrected noncentrality parameter is zero, which means there is not enough information in the prior result to plan the sample size as desired. With this prior result and 'alpha_prior', the largest 'assurance' that still yields a usable plan is about .93; re-run with 'assurance' at or below that value, or raise 'alpha_prior' to lift the ceiling. Re-running at a lower 'assurance' is not free: the plan it returns carries that lower assurance, not the one you first asked for, so the long run proportion of replications reaching your target power falls accordingly. 'alpha_prior' does not change the prior study, which is what it is; it is your assumption about the publication threshold the study's literature faced, so raising it toward 1 assumes less publication bias to undo (for example, 'alpha_prior = .10' assumes the literature's journals would have published a result significant at the .10 level, a more lenient policy than .05, and 'alpha_prior = 1' assumes no publication bias at all). See Anderson, Kelley, and Maxwell (2017) and Anderson and Kelley (2024).

This function does not apply to an omnibus fit chi square: the correction assumes a literature publishes significant results, whereas a publishable fit chi square is a small (nonsignificant) one, which inverts the selection region the method is built on. A just-identified full model also has 0 degrees of freedom; if that is your case and the comparison is a genuine difference test, the plan depends only on the number of constraints, so call with 'df_full = 1' and 'df_restricted' equal to 1 plus the number of constraints.  # Requesting more assurance than the prior result can support stops with an # informative error naming the largest workable assurance (here near .95): try(ss_buc_chisq_diff(chisq_observed = 9.5, N = 250, df_full = 42,   df_restricted = 43, assurance = .99)) #> Error : Sample size planning is not possible with these settings. code: result <- ss_buc_correlation(r_observed = .35, N = 100, alpha_prior = .05,   alpha_planned = .05, assurance = .80, desired_power = .80) result #>  term          value #>  necessary_N   122   #>  actual_power  0.802 #>  ncp_adjusted  6.71  #>  rho_planning  0.251 #>  r_observed    0.35  #>  N             100   #>  alpha_prior   0.05  #>  alpha_planned 0.05  #>  assurance     0.8   #>  desired_power 0.8   #>  #> Design: Pearson correlation #> Sample size unit: total #> Largest supportable assurance: .99  # The equivalent call from the observed t statistic: ss_buc_correlation(t_observed = .35 * sqrt(98 / (1 - .35^2)), N = 100) #>  term          value #>  necessary_N   122   #>  actual_power  0.802 #>  ncp_adjusted  6.71  #>  rho_planning  0.251 #>  t_observed    3.7   #>  N             100   #>  alpha_prior   0.05  #>  alpha_planned 0.05  #>  assurance     0.8   #>  desired_power 0.8   #>  #> Design: Pearson correlation #> Sample size unit: total #> Largest supportable assurance: .99  # Requesting more assurance than the prior result can support stops with an # informative error naming the largest workable assurance. The correlation # above supports .99, so a weaker prior is needed to reach the ceiling # (here near .86): try(ss_buc_correlation(r_observed = .27, N = 100, assurance = .95)) #> Error : Sample size planning is not possible with these settings. After correcting the prior study's effect for publication bias and uncertainty at the requested level of assurance, the corrected noncentrality parameter is zero, which means there is not enough information in the prior result to plan the sample size as desired. With this prior result and 'alpha_prior', the largest 'assurance' that still yields a usable plan is about .86; re-run with 'assurance' at or below that value, or raise 'alpha_prior' to lift the ceiling. Re-running at a lower 'assurance' is not free: the plan it returns carries that lower assurance, not the one you first asked for, so the long run proportion of replications reaching your target power falls accordingly. 'alpha_prior' does not change the prior study, which is what it is; it is your assumption about the publication threshold the study's literature faced, so raising it toward 1 assumes less publication bias to undo (for example, 'alpha_prior = .10' assumes the literature's journals would have published a result significant at the .10 level, a more lenient policy than .05, and 'alpha_prior = 1' assumes no publication bias at all). See Anderson, Kelley, and Maxwell (2017) and Anderson and Kelley (2024).

After correcting the prior study's effect for publication bias and uncertainty at the requested level of assurance, the corrected noncentrality parameter is zero, which means there is not enough information in the prior result to plan the sample size as desired. With this prior result and 'alpha_prior', the largest 'assurance' that still yields a usable plan is about .83; re-run with 'assurance' at or below that value, or raise 'alpha_prior' to lift the ceiling. Re-running at a lower 'assurance' is not free: the plan it returns carries that lower assurance, not the one you first asked for, so the long run proportion of replications reaching your target power falls accordingly. 'alpha_prior' does not change the prior study, which is what it is; it is your assumption about the publication threshold the study's literature faced, so raising it toward 1 assumes less publication bias to undo (for example, 'alpha_prior = .10' assumes the literature's journals would have published a result significant at the .10 level, a more lenient policy than .05, and 'alpha_prior = 1' assumes no publication bias at all). See Anderson, Kelley, and Maxwell (2017) and Anderson and Kelley (2024).

code: result <- ss_buc_manova(F_observed = 4.5, N = 80, p_variables = 3,   alpha_prior = .05, alpha_planned = .05, assurance = .80,   desired_power = .80) result #>  term                  value  #>  necessary_n_per_group 310    #>  total_N               620    #>  actual_power          0.801  #>  ncp_adjusted          1.42   #>  D2_planning           0.0709 #>  F_observed            4.5    #>  N                     80     #>  p_variables           3      #>  alpha_prior           0.05   #>  alpha_planned         0.05   #>  assurance             0.8    #>  desired_power         0.8    #>  #> Design: Two-group multivariate comparison (Hotelling's T squared) #> Sample size unit: per group #> Largest supportable assurance: .88  # The equivalent call from Hotelling's T squared: ss_buc_manova(T2_observed = 4.5 * 3 * 78 / 76, N = 80, p_variables = 3) #>  term                  value  #>  necessary_n_per_group 310    #>  total_N               620    #>  actual_power          0.801  #>  ncp_adjusted          1.42   #>  D2_planning           0.0709 #>  T2_observed           13.9   #>  N                     80     #>  p_variables           3      #>  alpha_prior           0.05   #>  alpha_planned         0.05   #>  assurance             0.8    #>  desired_power         0.8    #>  #> Design: Two-group multivariate comparison (Hotelling's T squared) #> Sample size unit: per group #> Largest supportable assurance: .88  # Requesting more assurance than the prior result can support stops with an # informative error naming the largest workable assurance (here near .88): try(ss_buc_manova(F_observed = 4.5, N = 80, p_variables = 3,   assurance = .95)) #> Error : Sample size planning is not possible with these settings. After correcting the prior study's effect for publication bias and uncertainty at the requested level of assurance, the corrected noncentrality parameter is zero, which means there is not enough information in the prior result to plan the sample size as desired. With this prior result and 'alpha_prior', the largest 'assurance' that still yields a usable plan is about .88; re-run with 'assurance' at or below that value, or raise 'alpha_prior' to lift the ceiling. Re-running at a lower 'assurance' is not free: the plan it returns carries that lower assurance, not the one you first asked for, so the long run proportion of replications reaching your target power falls accordingly. 'alpha_prior' does not change the prior study, which is what it is; it is your assumption about the publication threshold the study's literature faced, so raising it toward 1 assumes less publication bias to undo (for example, 'alpha_prior = .10' assumes the literature's journals would have published a result significant at the .10 level, a more lenient policy than .05, and 'alpha_prior = 1' assumes no publication bias at all). See Anderson, Kelley, and Maxwell (2017) and Anderson and Kelley (2024).

Requesting more assurance than the prior result can support stops with an # informative error naming the largest workable assurance (here near .82): try(ss_buc_mixed_anova_general(F_observed = 5, N = 90, df_numerator = 2,   num_groups = 3, effect = "between_only",   assurance = .95)) #> Error : Sample size planning is not possible with these settings. After correcting the prior study's effect for publication bias and uncertainty at the requested level of assurance, the corrected noncentrality parameter is zero, which means there is not enough information in the prior result to plan the sample size as desired. With this prior result and 'alpha_prior', the largest 'assurance' that still yields a usable plan is about .82; re-run with 'assurance' at or below that value, or raise 'alpha_prior' to lift the ceiling. Re-running at a lower 'assurance' is not free: the plan it returns carries that lower assurance, not the one you first asked for, so the long run proportion of replications reaching your target power falls accordingly. 'alpha_prior' does not change the prior study, which is what it is; it is your assumption about the publication threshold the study's literature faced, so raising it toward 1 assumes less publication bias to undo (for example, 'alpha_prior = .10' assumes the literature's journals would have published a result significant at the .10 level, a more lenient policy than .05, and 'alpha_prior = 1' assumes no publication bias at all). See Anderson, Kelley, and Maxwell (2017) and Anderson and Kelley (2024).

After correcting the prior study's effect for publication bias and uncertainty at the requested level of assurance, the corrected noncentrality parameter is zero, which means there is not enough information in the prior result to plan the sample size as desired. With this prior result and 'alpha_prior', the largest 'assurance' that still yields a usable plan is about .94; re-run with 'assurance' at or below that value, or raise 'alpha_prior' to lift the ceiling. Re-running at a lower 'assurance' is not free: the plan it returns carries that lower assurance, not the one you first asked for, so the long run proportion of replications reaching your target power falls accordingly. 'alpha_prior' does not change the prior study, which is what it is; it is your assumption about the publication threshold the study's literature faced, so raising it toward 1 assumes less publication bias to undo (for example, 'alpha_prior = .10' assumes the literature's journals would have published a result significant at the .10 level, a more lenient policy than .05, and 'alpha_prior = 1' assumes no publication bias at all). See Anderson, Kelley, and Maxwell (2017) and Anderson and Kelley (2024).

code: result <- ss_buc_reg_coef(t_observed = 3, N = 150, p = 3, alpha_prior = .05,   alpha_planned = .05, assurance = .80, desired_power = .80) result #>  term              value  #>  necessary_N       624    #>  actual_power      0.8    #>  ncp_adjusted      1.89   #>  f2_planning       0.0126 #>  t_observed        3      #>  N                 150    #>  p                 3      #>  random_predictors 0      #>  alpha_prior       0.05   #>  alpha_planned     0.05   #>  assurance         0.8    #>  desired_power     0.8    #>  #> Design: Multiple regression: single coefficient #> Predictors: fixed by design #> Sample size unit: total #> Largest supportable assurance: .93  # Predictors sampled along with the outcome, as in most observational # research: ss_buc_reg_coef(t_observed = 3, N = 150, p = 3, random_predictors = TRUE) #>  term              value  #>  necessary_N       623    #>  actual_power      0.8    #>  ncp_adjusted      1.91   #>  f2_planning       0.0127 #>  t_observed        3      #>  N                 150    #>  p                 3      #>  random_predictors 1      #>  alpha_prior       0.05   #>  alpha_planned     0.05   #>  assurance         0.8    #>  desired_power     0.8    #>  #> Design: Multiple regression: single coefficient #> Predictors: random (sampled along with the outcome) #> Sample size unit: total #> Largest supportable assurance: .93  # Requesting more assurance than the prior result can support stops with an # informative error naming the largest workable assurance (here near .93): try(ss_buc_reg_coef(t_observed = 3, N = 150, p = 3, assurance = .95)) #> Error : Sample size planning is not possible with these settings. After correcting the prior study's effect for publication bias and uncertainty at the requested level of assurance, the corrected noncentrality parameter is zero, which means there is not enough information in the prior result to plan the sample size as desired. With this prior result and 'alpha_prior', the largest 'assurance' that still yields a usable plan is about .93; re-run with 'assurance' at or below that value, or raise 'alpha_prior' to lift the ceiling. Re-running at a lower 'assurance' is not free: the plan it returns carries that lower assurance, not the one you first asked for, so the long run proportion of replications reaching your target power falls accordingly. 'alpha_prior' does not change the prior study, which is what it is; it is your assumption about the publication threshold the study's literature faced, so raising it toward 1 assumes less publication bias to undo (for example, 'alpha_prior = .10' assumes the literature's journals would have published a result significant at the .10 level, a more lenient policy than .05, and 'alpha_prior = 1' assumes no publication bias at all). See Anderson, Kelley, and Maxwell (2017) and Anderson and Kelley (2024).

code: result <- ss_buc_rm_anova(F_observed = 5, N = 60, levels_A = 2, levels_B = 3,   effect = "factor_B", alpha_prior = .05, alpha_planned = .05,   assurance = .80, desired_power = .80) result #>  term          value  #>  necessary_N   1902   #>  actual_power  0.8    #>  ncp_adjusted  0.304  #>  f_planning    0.0504 #>  F_observed    5      #>  N             60     #>  levels_A      2      #>  levels_B      3      #>  epsilon       1      #>  alpha_prior   0.05   #>  alpha_planned 0.05   #>  assurance     0.8    #>  desired_power 0.8    #>  #> Design: One- or two-way within-subjects ANOVA (factor_B) #> Sample size unit: total #> Largest supportable assurance: .83  # A prior study reported with Greenhouse-Geisser corrected degrees of # freedom, 1.73 and 50.2, for a three-level factor with 30 subjects: the # correction is 1.73/2, and the plan is larger than under sphericity (92 # subjects). ss_buc_rm_anova(F_observed = 6.5, N = 30, levels_A = 3, epsilon = 1.73 / 2) #>  term          value #>  necessary_N   162   #>  actual_power  0.802 #>  ncp_adjusted  2     #>  f_planning    0.183 #>  F_observed    6.5   #>  N             30    #>  levels_A      3     #>  epsilon       0.865 #>  alpha_prior   0.05  #>  alpha_planned 0.05  #>  assurance     0.8   #>  desired_power 0.8   #>  #> Design: One- or two-way within-subjects ANOVA (factor_A) #> Sample size unit: total #> Largest supportable assurance: .90  # Requesting more assurance than the prior result can support stops with an # informative error naming the largest workable assurance (here near .83): try(ss_buc_rm_anova(F_observed = 5, N = 60, levels_A = 2, levels_B = 3,   effect = "factor_B", assurance = .95)) #> Error : Sample size planning is not possible with these settings. After correcting the prior study's effect for publication bias and uncertainty at the requested level of assurance, the corrected noncentrality parameter is zero, which means there is not enough information in the prior result to plan the sample size as desired. With this prior result and 'alpha_prior', the largest 'assurance' that still yields a usable plan is about .83; re-run with 'assurance' at or below that value, or raise 'alpha_prior' to lift the ceiling. Re-running at a lower 'assurance' is not free: the plan it returns carries that lower assurance, not the one you first asked for, so the long run proportion of replications reaching your target power falls accordingly. 'alpha_prior' does not change the prior study, which is what it is; it is your assumption about the publication threshold the study's literature faced, so raising it toward 1 assumes less publication bias to undo (for example, 'alpha_prior = .10' assumes the literature's journals would have published a result significant at the .10 level, a more lenient policy than .05, and 'alpha_prior = 1' assumes no publication bias at all). See Anderson, Kelley, and Maxwell (2017) and Anderson and Kelley (2024).

code: result <- ss_buc_rm_anova_general(F_observed = 6.5, N = 80, df_numerator = 1,   alpha_prior = .05, alpha_planned = .05, assurance = .50, desired_power = .80) result #>  term          value #>  necessary_N   256   #>  actual_power  0.8   #>  ncp_adjusted  2.47  #>  f_planning    0.176 #>  F_observed    6.5   #>  N             80    #>  df_numerator  1     #>  epsilon       1     #>  alpha_prior   0.05  #>  alpha_planned 0.05  #>  assurance     0.5   #>  desired_power 0.8   #>  #> Design: Within-subjects ANOVA (any number of factors) #> Sample size unit: total #> Largest supportable assurance: .74  # A prior study reported with Greenhouse-Geisser corrected degrees of # freedom, 1.4 and 40.6, for an effect with 2 numerator degrees of freedom # and 30 subjects: the correction is 1.4/2 (under sphericity, the plan is # 46 subjects). ss_buc_rm_anova_general(F_observed = 8, N = 30, df_numerator = 2,   epsilon = .7) #>  term          value #>  necessary_N   109   #>  actual_power  0.801 #>  ncp_adjusted  3.47  #>  f_planning    0.241 #>  F_observed    8     #>  N             30    #>  df_numerator  2     #>  epsilon       0.7   #>  alpha_prior   0.05  #>  alpha_planned 0.05  #>  assurance     0.8   #>  desired_power 0.8   #>  #> Design: Within-subjects ANOVA (any number of factors) #> Sample size unit: total #> Largest supportable assurance: .93  # Requesting more assurance than the prior result can support stops with an # informative error naming the largest workable assurance (here near .74): try(ss_buc_rm_anova_general(F_observed = 6.5, N = 80, df_numerator = 1,   assurance = .95)) #> Error : Sample size planning is not possible with these settings. After correcting the prior study's effect for publication bias and uncertainty at the requested level of assurance, the corrected noncentrality parameter is zero, which means there is not enough information in the prior result to plan the sample size as desired. With this prior result and 'alpha_prior', the largest 'assurance' that still yields a usable plan is about .74; re-run with 'assurance' at or below that value, or raise 'alpha_prior' to lift the ceiling. Re-running at a lower 'assurance' is not free: the plan it returns carries that lower assurance, not the one you first asked for, so the long run proportion of replications reaching your target power falls accordingly. 'alpha_prior' does not change the prior study, which is what it is; it is your assumption about the publication threshold the study's literature faced, so raising it toward 1 assumes less publication bias to undo (for example, 'alpha_prior = .10' assumes the literature's journals would have published a result significant at the .10 level, a more lenient policy than .05, and 'alpha_prior = 1' assumes no publication bias at all). See Anderson, Kelley, and Maxwell (2017) and Anderson and Kelley (2024).

Requesting more assurance than the prior result can support stops with an # informative error naming the largest workable assurance (here near .93): try(ss_buc_welch_t(t_observed = 3, n_1 = 40, n_2 = 55, sd_ratio = 1.5,   assurance = .95)) #> Error : Sample size planning is not possible with these settings. After correcting the prior study's effect for publication bias and uncertainty at the requested level of assurance, the corrected noncentrality parameter is zero, which means there is not enough information in the prior result to plan the sample size as desired. With this prior result and 'alpha_prior', the largest 'assurance' that still yields a usable plan is about .93; re-run with 'assurance' at or below that value, or raise 'alpha_prior' to lift the ceiling. Re-running at a lower 'assurance' is not free: the plan it returns carries that lower assurance, not the one you first asked for, so the long run proportion of replications reaching your target power falls accordingly. 'alpha_prior' does not change the prior study, which is what it is; it is your assumption about the publication threshold the study's literature faced, so raising it toward 1 assumes less publication bias to undo (for example, 'alpha_prior = .10' assumes the literature's journals would have published a result significant at the .10 level, a more lenient policy than .05, and 'alpha_prior = 1' assumes no publication bias at all). See Anderson, Kelley, and Maxwell (2017) and Anderson and Kelley (2024).
